claims.text: Under rapid heating and cooling, the balance between mixing enthalpy and atomic mobility governs whether noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles form a single-phase solid solution.
Atomic mobility is driven by the heating rate.
A slower heating ramp with an intermediate-temperature dwell favors full elemental interdiffusion.
A slower heating ramp with an intermediate-temperature dwell suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
Very rapid heating and cooling kinetically traps the nanoparticles in multiphase states.
Ultra-rapid thermal processing of these nanoparticles tends to produce phase separation.
Ultra-rapid thermal processing of these nanoparticles tends to produce elemental segregation.
Ultra-rapid thermal processing of these nanoparticles tends to produce uncontrolled particle morphology.
Atomic diffusion kinetics, mixing enthalpy, and size-mismatch strain mediate structural evolution toward a uniform single-phase state.
A slower heating rate and intermediate dwell provide enough time for atoms to overcome local energy barriers.
Overcoming local energy barriers through the moderated thermal profile leads to elemental homogenization.
Rapid processing freezes elemental inhomogeneities and segregation into the nanoparticles.
Frozen elemental inhomogeneities and segregation lead to multiphase particles.
The slower controlled thermal profile will produce a more uniform crystal structure than the rapid-processing baseline.
The slower controlled thermal profile will reduce elemental segregation relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
The slower controlled thermal profile will improve control of particle morphology relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies when the constituent noble metals have compatible or moderately exothermic mixing enthalpies.
The proposed mechanism may fail when elemental size mismatch or segregation tendencies are too extreme.
The proposed mechanism may fail when atomic mobility is intrinsically low.
